## Sources

## Prerequisites

Answer the following questions to see if you can bypass
this chapter. You can find the answers at the end of the
chapter in @sec-quiz-answers-18.

1. What is the primary purpose of a pre-registered
   Statistical Analysis Plan (SAP)?
2. Name at least five sections every clinical SAP
   should contain.
3. Why is it important, both scientifically and
   ethically, to distinguish pre-specified from
   exploratory analyses in the body of a SAP?

## Learning objectives

By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

- Draft a SAP using a standard section template, such
  as the published guideline of Gamble et al.
  [-@gamble2017sap], as a starting point.
- Pre-specify primary, secondary, and exploratory
  analyses with enough detail that a collaborator
  could execute them without further instruction.
- Compute sample-size requirements with `zzpower` and
  report them in the SAP.
- Define missing-data strategies, sensitivity
  analyses, and multiple-testing corrections
  explicitly.
- Version-control the SAP and tag the submitted
  version before data access.
- Distinguish pre-specified from exploratory analyses
  in the analysis plan and the eventual paper.

## Orientation

The SAP is, we would contend, the professional
biostatistician's most important non-code document, and the
argument for it is narrower and stronger than the one usually
made. It is not primarily a defense against dishonesty. Very
few analysts set out to select the analysis that gives the
answer they wanted. What they do, having looked at the data, is
make a long series of small and individually defensible
choices. Each is one they would have made differently had the
data looked otherwise, and none is experienced as a choice at
all. The p-value that emerges at the end has a
nominal Type-I error rate that assumes none of this happened.

A plan written before the data are seen is the only instrument
that distinguishes the two situations after the fact, because
by then the analyst's memory of what they would have done is
not evidence. Federally funded trials require one, most
journals require one for confirmatory analyses, and the reason
to want one has less to do with either than with being able to
say, truthfully, which of your findings the study was designed
to test.

The SAP exists to constrain analyst degrees of
freedom. Without it, the analysis plan is whatever
the analyst chose after looking at the data, and the
nominal Type-I error rate of the reported tests is
not what the math says it is. With it, the analysis
is anchored to a written-down plan that is on the
public record.

## The statistician's contribution {#sec-analysis-plan-human}

The SAP is judgment work, not boilerplate.

**Specify enough to constrain.** A SAP that says 'we
will fit a regression model' has not specified
anything. A SAP that says 'multivariable logistic
regression of 30-day readmission or death on
randomized arm (home health vs. usual care),
adjusted for age (continuous), sex, ejection
fraction (continuous), and discharge
medication count (continuous), with a 5% Type-I
error rate, two-sided' has constrained the
researcher degrees of freedom that matter. Aim for
the second.

**Pre-specify what you commit to.** A primary
analysis is a commitment. The Type-I error rate of
that test is the rate the reader is told. Adding
sensitivity analyses, exploratory analyses, and
'data-prompted' analyses afterward is fine,
provided they are labeled as such. Mixing them with
the primary changes what the primary actually means.

**Be honest about uncertainty in the plan.** When
you do not know whether an assumption will hold,
pre-specify a method that remains valid either way
rather than a test that chooses between methods. 'If
the residuals show heteroscedasticity, we will use
HC1 standard errors; otherwise classical SEs' looks
careful but is a pretest procedure: the combined
rule's error rate is that of neither branch, and
classical SEs chosen after a heteroscedasticity test
that lacked power are the worst of both. 'We will
use HC3 standard errors' commits to an estimator
that is valid whether or not the variance is
constant and costs little when it is
[@long2000hc]. 'We will use SEs' constrains
nothing.

**Tag the SAP at data access.** Git tag
`sap-v1.0-locked` at the moment the data become
accessible. The tag is the proof of pre-
specification. Later amendments are dated tags
(`sap-v1.1-amendment-1`); their relationship to the
data-access timeline is auditable.

These judgments are what make a SAP a serious
document rather than a regulatory chore.

## Why pre-register?

The case rests on three observations:

1. **Researcher degrees of freedom inflate Type-I
   error.** With many possible analyses (which
   covariates to include, which transformations,
   which subgroups), the chance that *some* analysis
   produces $p < 0.05$ under the null is much
   greater than 5%. Simmons, Nelson, and Simonsohn
   [-@simmons2011false] calculate that four
   commonly-encountered degrees of freedom inflate
   Type-I error from 5% to about 60%.

2. **The 'garden of forking paths'**
   [@gelman2013garden]: even without conscious p-hacking,
   the analysis is data-driven if the analyst made
   choices in response to early data exploration.
   The reported test's calibration depends on the
   *unmade* choices that would have been made on
   different data.

3. **Pre-registration constrains the choices.** A
   SAP written before data access fixes the
   covariates, the model class, the missingness
   strategy, the multiple-comparison correction. The
   eventual analysis is what was pre-specified; any
   deviation is documented as an amendment or as
   exploratory.

The trade-off is honest: pre-registration restricts
flexibility. The flexibility it restricts was
producing inflated false-positive rates anyway.

## A SAP template

A standard biostatistical SAP has these sections.
The list is a condensed version of the published
guideline for the content of clinical-trial SAPs
[@gamble2017sap], which is the fuller checklist to
use for a trial:

1. **Background and rationale.** Why this study, in
   half a page. Sets the audience for the rest.
2. **Research questions and hypotheses.** Numbered.
   Each question paired with the specific
   statistical hypothesis it implies.
3. **Study design.** RCT (parallel, crossover,
   cluster), observational cohort, case-control,
   etc. Sample size and power justification reference
   this design.
4. **Inclusion and exclusion criteria.** As a numbered
   list. Each criterion testable from data alone.
5. **Primary outcome definition.** Operationalized:
   the data fields, the time window, the value
   transformation. A second analyst should compute
   the same outcome variable.
6. **Secondary outcomes.** Same level of detail.
7. **Covariates.** Each one named, with its
   transformation if any (continuous? categorized?
   reference level?). Effects of interest specified.
8. **Primary analysis.** Specific test or model.
   Expected output (point estimate, CI, p-value).
   Type-I error rate.
9. **Secondary analyses.** Each one its own subsection
   with the same level of detail.
10. **Sensitivity analyses.** Each labeled as
    sensitivity (e.g., 'sensitivity to missing-data
    assumption'); pre-specified, not data-driven.
11. **Missing-data handling.** Specific strategy:
    complete-case, multiple imputation, IPW; the
    assumed mechanism (MCAR, MAR, MNAR); diagnostic
    checks.
12. **Multiple testing.** Family-wise correction
    (Bonferroni, Holm, fixed-sequence or other
    gatekeeping procedures) or false discovery
    rate (BH) procedure; the family of tests it
    applies to.
13. **Reporting.** What gets reported, in what
    table/figure, in what manuscript.

The template is a checklist; not every section is
needed for every study. For an observational
secondary analysis, sections 3 and 4 are simpler;
sections 8--12 are the same.

The template says what a SAP must contain. It does
not say whether the analysis it specifies is a good
one, and a SAP can be complete, version-controlled,
tagged before data access, and still pre-specify a
weak analysis. For that second question there is a
useful external cross-check: Harrell's author
checklist [@harrell2024checklist], maintained for
years as the Vanderbilt Biostatistics manuscript
checklist and now hosted on datamethods.org. It is
written for the reviewer of a finished manuscript,
which makes it the right instrument to run against a
draft SAP, because every item on it is a way a paper
gets rejected that a plan could have prevented. Its
recurring targets are decisions this template invites
you to make in section 7 and section 8. They include
categorizing a continuous covariate rather than modeling
it with a spline, selecting variables by stepwise
procedures, reporting a p-value without the interval
that gives it magnitude, and choosing a sample size
from an effect size observed in a previous study rather
than from the effect worth detecting. *Regression Modeling
Strategies* [@harrell2015rms] is the book-length
argument behind those items. Read the checklist once
before you draft section 8, and again after.

The first argument names a design from the package's
registry. Besides `ttest_2groups` it holds
`ttest_paired`, `ttest_one_sample`, `prop_2groups`,
`correlation`, `logrank`, `fisher_exact`, `trend_prop`,
`anova_oneway`, `mcnemar`, `mixed_model`, and
`cluster_rct`, which covers most of what a clinical SAP
needs. Supplying `target_power` solves for sample size;
supplying `sample_size` solves for power.

To see the trade-off rather than a single number, which
is usually what a protocol discussion actually wants,
`power_table()` sweeps a grid of effect sizes against

::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

            effect_grid      = seq(0.3, 0.8, by = 0.1),
            power_thresholds = c(0.80, 0.90),
            effect_method    = "cohens_d")

:::


In the SAP, report the sample size with the
underlying assumptions, and apply the attrition
assumption rather than merely stating it. The
calculation gives the number of participants who
must be *analyzed*; the number enrolled has to be
larger by the factor $1/(1 - \text{attrition})$:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
attrition  <- 0.10
n_analyzed <- power.t.test(delta = 0.5, sd = 1,
                           power = 0.80)$n
n_enrolled <- ceiling(n_analyzed / (1 - attrition))

c(analyzed = ceiling(n_analyzed), enrolled = n_enrolled)
#> analyzed enrolled 
#>       64       71
```
:::


> The study will enroll 71 participants
> per arm (142 in total), so that
> with 10% attrition 64 per arm
> remain for analysis, giving 80% power to detect a
> standardized effect of 0.5 at a two-sided
> $\alpha = 0.05$.

A plan that says '64 per arm, assuming 10%
attrition' and enrolls 64 has assumed the attrition
and then ignored it.

If the assumptions are uncertain, present a table of
required sample sizes under several effect sizes,
and choose the planned sample size based on
feasibility.

## Pre-specified vs. exploratory

A pre-specified analysis is one that:

- Was written down in the SAP before data access.
- Has its statistical properties (Type-I error rate,
  CI coverage) calibrated to the SAP's specification,
  not to the analyst's choices afterward.
- Carries the full inferential authority of the
  study.

An exploratory analysis is one that:

- Was generated after seeing the data, or that was
  not pre-specified for some reason (a reviewer
  request, an unexpected finding).
- Has its statistical properties uncalibrated.
- Is hypothesis-generating, not confirmatory.

In the SAP, separate them clearly:

> **Pre-specified analyses.** [list]
>
> **Exploratory analyses (hypothesis-generating,
> reported with appropriate caution).** [list]

In the paper, label them in the methods section:

> The primary analysis was a multivariable logistic
> regression of 30-day readmission or death on
> randomized arm, pre-specified in the analysis plan
> (Supplementary Material, version 1.0). Subgroup
> analyses by age were exploratory and are reported
> as hypothesis-generating.

The convention spares the reader from over-
interpreting exploratory findings while preserving
their scientific value as motivation for follow-up.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: pre-spec vs. exploratory

**Question.** You have pre-specified a primary
logistic regression. Reviewers ask for a subgroup
analysis by age. You run it and find a significant
interaction. How should this appear in the paper?

**Answer.**

The subgroup analysis is exploratory because it was
not pre-specified. Even though the data showed a
significant interaction, the test's Type-I error
rate is not 5% in any meaningful sense: the test
was selected after the data were seen. Report the
result clearly labeled as exploratory and
hypothesis-generating, not as a confirmatory
finding. The interaction is a candidate for a
future pre-registered study; in the current paper,
it joins the discussion section as an interesting
observation, not the results section as a
confirmatory test. Mislabelling exploratory
findings as confirmatory is among the most common
forms of inferential overreach in clinical
research.

:::

## Version control and tagging

A SAP that can be edited after the data arrive is not a
pre-specification, whatever it says on its front page.
What makes the claim checkable is a timestamped tag in a
history nobody can quietly rewrite. @fig-sap-timeline is
the sequence that has to hold.

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%| label: fig-sap-timeline
%%| fig-alt: "Left-to-right timeline. Drafting the SAP with no data
%%|   access leads to an immutable pushed git tag sap-v1.0, then to
%%|   data lock and unblinding, then to analysis, then to a report
%%|   that labels results pre-specified or exploratory. A dashed
%%|   branch from the data lock shows an amendment made after data
%%|   access, tagged sap-v1.1 and marked exploratory unless
%%|   justified and dated, rejoining the analysis."
%%| fig-cap: "The SAP against the data timeline. Everything to the
%%|   left of the lock is pre-specified and carries the study's
%%|   inferential authority. Anything written after it is
%%|   exploratory, and an amendment made after data access must be
%%|   tagged as its own version so that the order of events stays
%%|   auditable."
flowchart LR
  D["Draft SAP<br/><i>no data access</i>"]
  D --> T1["<b>git tag sap-v1.0</b><br/><i>pushed, immutable</i>"]
  T1 --> L["Data lock<br/>and unblinding"]
  L --> A["Analysis<br/><i>executes the plan</i>"]
  A --> R["Report<br/><i>labels pre-specified<br/>vs exploratory</i>"]
  L -.->|"amendment after<br/>data access"| T2["<b>git tag sap-v1.1</b><br/><i>exploratory unless<br/>justified and dated</i>"]
  T2 -.-> A
```

The SAP lives in the project's Git repository:

```
project/
├── SAP/
│   ├── sap-v1.0.qmd       # current SAP
│   ├── sap-v1.0.pdf       # rendered version submitted to ClinicalTrials.gov
│   └── amendments/
│       ├── amendment-1.qmd
│       └── amendment-2.qmd
└── ...
```

Tag the moment of data lock:

```bash
git tag -a sap-v1.0-locked -m "SAP locked at data access 2026-04-23"
git push origin sap-v1.0-locked
```

Later amendments are separate commits and tags:

```bash
git tag -a sap-v1.1-amendment-1 -m "Amendment 1: revised missing-data strategy following blinded data review"
```

Amendments must be made before unblinded data
analysis to retain confirmatory status; amendments
made after unblinding (after seeing outcomes) are
exploratory by definition.

For trials, deposit the locked SAP at the trial
registry (ClinicalTrials.gov, ANZCTR, ISRCTN) at
the time of registration. The deposited copy is the
authoritative pre-specification.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: a tag you could have forged

**Question.** You tag the SAP `sap-v1.0` before data lock,
as this chapter recommends. A skeptical reviewer points out
that `git tag` can be created at any time with any name,
and that you could have written the tag last week after
seeing the results. What actually stops you?

**Answer.**

Locally, nothing. The reviewer is right about the
mechanism and wrong about the conclusion, and it is worth
knowing which is which.

A tag is a label on a commit and can be created, deleted
and moved at will. Commit dates are metadata a determined
person can set. A repository sitting on your laptop proves
nothing about *when*, only about *what*.

What supplies the timing is publication to somewhere you
do not control. Pushing the tag to a remote creates a
record on a server with its own timestamps and its own
log. The registry deposit above is stronger still, since
ClinicalTrials.gov records a submission date you cannot
edit. Stronger again is anything that timestamps content
cryptographically, such as a Zenodo DOI or an OSF
registration.

So the honest statement of the practice is: the tag makes
the pre-specification *findable and unambiguous*, and an
external record makes it *credible*. The chapter's
instruction to push the tag rather than merely create it is
carrying the whole weight, and a SAP tagged but never
pushed provides organization without evidence.

This is the same distinction @sec-federal draws between
hosting an artifact and depositing it.
:::

## Worked example: SAP outline

The design numbers in the plan below are computed,
not typed, from four assumptions: a 25% event rate
under usual care, a 5-point absolute reduction worth
detecting, 80% power at two-sided $\alpha = 0.05$,
and up to 10% of patients without an ascertainable
outcome.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
p_usual    <- 0.25
p_home     <- 0.20
missing_hf <- 0.10

hf_design <- power.prop.test(p1 = p_usual, p2 = p_home,
                             power = 0.80)
n_eval    <- ceiling(hf_design$n)
n_rand    <- ceiling(hf_design$n / (1 - missing_hf))
or_hf     <- (p_home / (1 - p_home)) /
  (p_usual / (1 - p_usual))
power_750 <- power.prop.test(n = 750, p1 = p_usual,
                             p2 = p_home)$power

c(evaluable_per_arm  = n_eval,
  randomized_per_arm = n_rand,
  randomized_total   = 2 * n_rand)
#>  evaluable_per_arm randomized_per_arm   randomized_total 
#>               1094               1216               2432
round(c(odds_ratio = or_hf, power_at_750 = power_750), 2)
#>   odds_ratio power_at_750 
#>         0.75         0.64
```
:::


The last line is a warning about typed numbers. An
earlier draft of this plan read '1500 (750 per arm)
for 80% power to detect OR = 0.75 at baseline rate
0.25'. At those rates 750 per arm gives
64% power, not 80%, and no one
checking the prose by eye would have noticed.

> **Title:** Statistical Analysis Plan for the
> Effect of Post-Discharge Home Health Visits on
> 30-Day Readmission or Death in Heart Failure
> (HF-HOME-RCT)
>
> **Version:** 1.0, locked 2026-04-23.
>
> ## 1. Background
>
> Patients hospitalized with heart failure have a
> 30-day risk of readmission or death of about 25%. Home-health visits
> within 7 days of discharge have been associated
> with reduced readmission in observational studies
> [...]. We test the causal effect with a parallel-
> group RCT.
>
> ## 2. Research question and estimand
>
> Among adults discharged alive after a heart-failure
> admission, does assignment to a home-health
> program (at least one visit within 7 days of
> discharge), compared with usual care, reduce the
> 30-day risk of readmission or death? The estimand,
> by its five ICH E9(R1) attributes
> [@ich2019e9r1]:
>
> - *Population:* patients meeting section 4.
> - *Treatment conditions:* assignment to the
>   home-health program versus usual care.
> - *Variable:* all-cause readmission or death
>   within 30 days of index discharge (section 5).
> - *Intercurrent events:* death before readmission
>   is handled by a composite strategy (it is an
>   event), so the variable is defined for every
>   patient. Not receiving the visit in the
>   home-health arm, and receiving home health
>   outside the protocol in the usual-care arm, are
>   handled by a treatment-policy strategy: patients
>   are analyzed as randomized, whatever they
>   received.
> - *Population-level summary:* the marginal risk
>   difference, usual care minus home health, so
>   that a positive value is a reduction.
>
> ## 3. Design
>
> Parallel-group, individually randomized, open-
> label RCT. 1:1 allocation. Stratified by site and
> baseline ejection fraction.
>
> ## 4. Eligibility
>
> Inclusion: (a) admitted with primary diagnosis
> heart failure (ICD-10 I50.x); (b) age $\geq 18$;
> (c) discharged alive.
> Exclusion: (a) hospice; (b) inability to consent;
> (c) prior enrollment in this trial.
>
> ## 5. Primary outcome
>
> Binary: all-cause readmission or death within 30
> days of index discharge. Readmission is any
> inpatient admission to any institution. Source:
> institutional EHR linked to the state HIE and to
> state death records.
>
> ## 8. Primary analysis
>
> Logistic regression of the primary outcome on
> randomized arm (as randomized, never as treatment
> received), adjusted for age (continuous), sex,
> ejection fraction (continuous), discharge
> medication count (continuous), and site (fixed
> effect, as a stratification factor). The arm
> coefficient of this model is a *conditional* odds
> ratio and is not the estimand. The estimand is
> obtained by standardization (g-computation):
> predict each randomized patient's risk under each
> arm, average over all randomized patients, and
> take the difference. 95% CI by nonparametric
> bootstrap (2,000 resamples, percentile). Two-sided
> $\alpha = 0.05$. The conditional odds ratio is
> reported as a supportive summary, labeled as
> conditional.
>
> Sample size: 1,094
> evaluable patients per arm give 80% power to
> detect a reduction from 25% to
> 20% (odds ratio
> 0.75) at two-sided
> $\alpha = 0.05$ (`power.prop.test`). Allowing for
> up to 10% of patients without an
> ascertainable outcome, we randomize
> 1,216 per arm
> (2,432 in total).
>
> ## 11. Missing data
>
> Outcome: missing only for patients who cannot be
> linked to the state HIE (for example, after moving
> out of state). Primary: the standardized estimator
> of section 8, fitted to patients with an
> ascertained outcome and averaged over all
> randomized patients, which is valid if
> missingness is independent of the outcome given
> arm and the adjustment covariates. Sensitivity:
> delta-adjustment tipping-point analysis. In the
> home-health arm, unascertained patients are
> assigned a risk $\delta$ times that of their
> observed peers, with $\delta$ increased from 1
> until the 95% CI includes zero; in the usual-care
> arm they are assigned the observed risk. Missing
> patients stay in the denominator. Covariates:
> $<5\%$ missing expected; imputed by the pooled
> mean (continuous) or mode (categorical), which is
> valid for baseline covariates in a randomized
> trial.
>
> ## 12. Multiple testing
>
> Primary outcome at two-sided $\alpha = 0.05$.
> Secondary outcomes by a fixed-sequence
> (hierarchical) procedure, in this order:
> (S1) 30-day all-cause readmission alone;
> (S2) 30-day emergency department visit;
> (S3) 90-day readmission or death. Each is tested
> at $\alpha = 0.05$ only if the primary and every
> earlier secondary test rejected; at the first
> non-rejection testing stops, and the remaining
> outcomes are reported as estimates with CIs and
> no p-value. This controls the familywise error
> rate at 0.05 across the primary and secondary
> outcomes. Testing the primary at 0.05 and the
> secondaries at Bonferroni-corrected levels
> regardless of the primary result does not: the
> two families each spend 0.05, and the familywise
> rate can approach 0.10.

This level of specificity is what 'pre-specified'
means. Vagueness invites researcher degrees of
freedom.

## Collaborating with an LLM on SAPs

LLMs draft SAP boilerplate well; the substantive
choices need human judgment.

**Prompt 1: drafting boilerplate sections.** Paste
the project description and ask: 'draft sections
1--4 of a SAP following the Gamble et al. (2017)
guideline for SAP content.'

*What to watch for.* The output will likely be the
right shape. Verify the inclusion/exclusion
criteria are checkable from data alone (no
'eligible at investigator discretion'). Verify the
outcome definition is operational.

*Verification.* Hand the draft to a clinical
collaborator; ask whether the outcome and
eligibility could be applied without further
instruction.

**Prompt 2: classifying analyses.** Paste a list of
analyses and ask: 'which are pre-specified
(confirmatory) and which are exploratory?'

*What to watch for.* The classification depends on
when each analysis was decided. The LLM cannot
know this; it can only flag analyses that look
exploratory in nature (subgroup, post-hoc).
Cross-check with your timeline.

*Verification.* For each analysis, ask: 'was this
in the SAP at data access?' If yes,
pre-specified; if no, exploratory.

**Prompt 3: power calculation.** Describe the
design and effect size; ask the LLM to compute
required sample size and to verify against
`zzpower`.

*What to watch for.* The LLM may produce a
formula-based answer that disagrees with `zzpower`.
The reasons are usually different assumptions
(unbalanced allocation, attrition, paired vs.
unpaired). Reconcile by stating assumptions
explicitly.

*Verification.* Compute by hand for a simple case;
verify the LLM and `zzpower` agree.

## Principle in use

Three habits make a plan binding rather than decorative:

1. **Specify with enough detail that a second
   analyst would produce the same result.** Vague
   pre-specification is barely pre-specification.
2. **Tag the SAP at data access.** Git tag plus
   trial-registry deposit gives an audit trail of
   when the analysis was committed.
3. **Distinguish pre-specified from exploratory in
   the paper.** Reader interpretation of evidence
   strength depends on this label.

## Exercises

1. Use `zzpower` to compute the required sample
   size for a two-arm comparison under three
   plausible effect sizes (small, medium, large).
   Then inflate each for a cluster randomized
   design with 20 patients per practice and an
   intracluster correlation of 0.02, and report
   the number of clusters required.

**Documents, not computations.** No answer key; a good
answer is a document, and what makes it good is stated
rather than computed.

2. Draft a SAP (skeleton only) for a hypothetical
   cluster randomized trial of a patient-education
   intervention. Use the template above, and include
   the table from exercise 1.
3. Locate a published paper with a publicly
   available SAP. Audit whether the paper's
   analyses match the SAP. Identify any deviations;
   classify them as amendments, exploratory, or
   unreported.
4. Take an analysis you completed without a SAP and
   write a retrospective SAP describing what should
   have been pre-specified. Note which choices were
   data-driven; flag those as exploratory.
5. Write an amendment to a SAP that revises the
   missing-data strategy following a blinded data
   review. Tag both versions in git; verify the
   timeline is auditable.

## Solution to exercise 1

**The individual-level requirement first.**


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(zzpower)

per_arm <- vapply(
  c(small = 0.2, medium = 0.5, large = 0.8),
  \(d) power_calc("ttest_2groups",
                  target_power  = 0.80,
                  effect_size   = d,
                  effect_method = "cohens_d",
                  alpha         = 0.05)$sample_sizes$n,
  numeric(1))

ceiling(per_arm)          # analytic n per arm
#>  small medium  large 
#>    394     64     26
```
:::


Note `sample_sizes` rather than `sample_size`: the element
is a list, because a two-arm calculation returns per-arm
and total figures separately, along with an ITT-inflated
version. Reading `$n` gives the analytic requirement per
arm, which is what the design effect below scales.

**Then the design effect.** A cluster randomized trial
does not randomize patients; it randomizes practices, and
patients within a practice resemble one another. The
variance inflation is
$\text{DEFF} = 1 + (m - 1)\rho$, with $m$ patients per
cluster and $\rho$ the intracluster correlation:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
m   <- 20      # patients per practice
rho <- 0.02    # intracluster correlation

deff <- 1 + (m - 1) * rho

total <- 2 * per_arm                 # both arms

data.frame(
  effect       = names(per_arm),
  n_total      = ceiling(total),
  deff         = round(deff, 2),
  n_cluster    = ceiling(total * deff),
  clusters     = ceiling(ceiling(total * deff) / m),
  row.names    = NULL
)
#>   effect n_total deff n_cluster clusters
#> 1  small     788 1.38      1087       55
#> 2 medium     128 1.38       177        9
#> 3  large      52 1.38        71        4
```
:::


An intracluster correlation of 0.02 sounds negligible and
is not. With 20 patients per practice it inflates the
required sample by 38%, because the design effect depends
on $\rho$ and cluster size jointly. Doubling the cluster
size to 40 would inflate it by 78% instead, so recruiting
more patients per practice buys progressively less.

Two things belong in the SAP alongside this table. The
value of $\rho$ is an assumption, not a measurement, and
it should be attributed to a source and given a
sensitivity range. And the number that gets recruited is
`clusters`, rounded up, so the realized sample is
generally larger than `n_cluster`; quoting the latter
as the target understates what the trial must enroll.
:::

## Prerequisites answers {#sec-quiz-answers-18}

1. The SAP locks in the analysis plan before data
   access, so that the eventual published results
   reflect hypotheses formed in advance rather than
   post-hoc choices made in the light of the data.
   It limits the 'garden of forking paths' that
   would otherwise inflate Type-I error and enable
   p-hacking. Federally funded trials require it;
   confirmatory analyses in any setting benefit
   from it.
2. (Any five of:) background and rationale;
   research questions and hypotheses; study design /
   cohort definition; inclusion/exclusion criteria;
   primary outcome definition; secondary outcomes;
   covariates; primary analysis; secondary
   analyses; sensitivity analyses; missing-data
   handling; multiple-testing correction; reporting/
   publication plan.
3. Pre-specified analyses represent commitments
   made before data access; they carry the full
   inferential authority of the study's sampling
   plan. Exploratory analyses are generated after
   seeing the data; they are hypothesis-generating,
   not confirmatory, and should be reported with
   appropriate caution. Conflating the two misleads
   readers about the evidential strength of the
   findings and is one of the most common sources
   of reproducibility failure in biomedical
   research.
